title: GNoME predicts 2.2 million crystal structures, of which few may be useful new compounds
summary: Google DeepMind's GNoME proposed 2.2 million crystal structures (380,000 stable); independent reviews (Cheetham & Seshadri 2024, Kurlin 2026) find duplicates and scant evidence of useful compounds.
account: On 29 November 2023 Google DeepMind published GNoME in Nature, reporting 2.2 million structures below the convex hull, calling it 'an order-of-magnitude expansion in stable materials known to humanity' and stating that 736 of the stable structures had already been independently realized; the company blog adds that the Berkeley Lab A-Lab synthesized more than 41 materials from the predictions. Cheetham and Seshadri (UC Santa Barbara, Chem. Mater., 8 April 2024) examined the listings and reported 'scant evidence for compounds that fulfill the trifecta of novelty, credibility, and utility'; 404 Media (11 April 2024) quoted Cheetham that the paper 'falls way short' as a practical contribution and DeepMind that it stands by all claims. C&EN (15 October 2026) reported an arXiv analysis by Vitaliy Kurlin (Liverpool) finding more than 15% near-duplicates within GNoME, about 24% duplicating Materials Project entries and about 17% close to ICSD entries, with Leslie Schoop (Princeton) calling some entries 'completely unrealistic'. The earlier verifier could not read the Chem. Mater. critique (HTTP 403); its abstract was fetched here through Europe PMC (PMC11044265). The date is the Nature publication date.
purpose: Predict stable inorganic crystal structures at scale to accelerate materials discovery
deployer: Google DeepMind (dataset released openly; stable structures contributed to the Materials Project)
taxonomy_note: Out of the biology theme but recorded under the no-discard rule. The primary paper and blog are vendor-authored; the only independent assessments fetched (Cheetham & Seshadri 2024; Kurlin via C&EN 2026) dispute novelty and utility, and no independently verified downstream material was found, so the record is a general benefit with all depths null.

ratings.reason: No individual beneficiary; a dataset release.
Use by the Materials Project and A-Lab is reported only by the vendor; independent reviewers find scant utility.
No demonstrated downstream technology; novelty of the predictions is disputed.

ai_role.statement: The graph-network model is the vendor's; its predictions are documented in a vendor-authored Nature paper and blog. Independent reviewers (Cheetham & Seshadri 2024; Kurlin 2026 as reported by C&EN) report near-duplicates, unrealistic compounds and little evidence of useful novel materials. Benefit therefore rests on the vendor's account and is contested.
